held_pairs.plain: Sometimes the answer differs significantly from what the questioner intended, whereas in written dialogue, the author has complete control over the answers. However, claiming that people in real life actually respond the way they are depicted here is a different matter. Socrates might call his interlocutors flexible young men because they answer the questions directly. These questions are crafted to make answering easy and to prevent any originality in the response. In the Socratic method shown by Plato and Xenophon, the responder respects the specific relationship established by the questioner. Critics object that in real life, we do not answer within that same relationship. Instead, we often introduce a different perspective. This approach certainly captures the spirit of a lively conversation, but such competitive spirit is excluded from the Socratic method, which focuses primarily on staying on topic. The attitude of dogmatism, self-assertion, stopping when difficulties arise, and escaping those difficulties through jokes or dismissal are all excluded here. These behaviors are not considered good manners and have no place in Socrates’ dialogues.
held_pairs.original: For the answer seems occasionally to be quite different from what was intended by the question, while in printed dialogue, answers are altogether under the author’s control; but to say that in actual life people are found to answer as they are here made to do, is quite another thing. To Socrates those who reply may be called pliable youths, because they reply directly to the questions, which are so formed that they make the answer very easy, and exclude any originality in reply. To this plastic manner, which we see in the method of Socrates, as represented by Plato and Xenophon, it is objected that we do not answer in the same relation in which the questioner asks; while, with Socrates, the relation which the questioner adopts is respected in the reply. The other way, which is to bring forward another point of view, is undoubtedly the spirit of an animated conversation, but such emulation is excluded from this Socratic method, in which the principal matter is to keep to the point. The spirit of dogmatism, self-assertion, stopping short when we seem to get into difficulties, and escaping from them by a jest, or by setting them aside—all these attitudes and methods are here excluded; they do not constitute good manners, nor do they have a place in Socrates’ dialogues.

held_pairs.plain: This marks a sharper break between the soul, understood as pure self-focus, and its prior state of natural, direct existence. It no longer shares an immediate identity with bodily nature; instead, the external body must first be brought into that role. Specific feelings can only take physical form in a very precise manner. The immediate part of the body serves as a specific possibility for a particular goal, representing a distinct aspect of its differentiated structure or a specific organ within its organic system. Shaping such a goal within the organic body reveals and expresses the “ideality” that is always latent in matter, particularly in that specific bodily part. This process allows the soul, characterized by its volitional and conceptual nature, to exist as substance within its corporeity. Consequently, an aptitude demonstrates that the body has become fully permeable and transformed into a tool. Thus, when a conception, such as a sequence of musical notes, resides in me, the body produces them accurately and effortlessly, without any resistance.
held_pairs.original: Thus comes out the more decided rupture between the soul as simple self-concentration, and its earlier naturalness and immediacy; it has lost its original and immediate identity with the bodily nature, and as external has first to be reduced to that position. Specific feelings can only get bodily shape in a perfectly specific way; and the immediate portion of body is a particular possibility for a specific aim (a particular aspect of its differentiated structure, a particular organ of its organic system). To mould such an aim in the organic body is to bring out and express the “ideality” which is implicit in matter always, and especially so in the specific bodily part, and thus to enable the soul, under its volitional and conceptual characters, to exist as substance in its corporeity. In this way an aptitude shows the corporeity rendered completely pervious, made into an instrument, so that when the conception (e.g. a series of musical notes) is in me, then without resistance and with ease the body gives them correct utterance.

held_pairs.plain: Were the logical structures of the concept truly empty, passive containers for ideas, indifferent to their contents, understanding them would be a pointless pursuit that truth could easily ignore. In reality, as structural aspects of the concept, they constitute the living essence of the real world. Only what is true because of, through, and within these structures is genuinely true in the actual world. However, the validity of these structures has never been analyzed for its own sake, nor has their essential connection been investigated. (a) The Concept as Concept. The Concept as Concept comprises three functional components or moments. (1) The first is Universality, which signifies that it maintains free equality with itself regarding its specific nature. (2) The second is Particularity, defined as that specific nature, where the universal remains calmly identical to itself. (3) The third is Individuality, representing the self-reflection of the specific natures of universality and particularity; this negative self-unity possesses full and primary determinateness, without diminishing its self-identity or universality.
held_pairs.original: If the logical forms of the notion were really dead and inert receptacles of conceptions and thoughts, careless of what they contained, knowledge about them would be an idle curiosity which the truth might dispense with. On the contrary they really are, as forms of the notion, the vital spirit of the actual world. That only is true of the actual which is true in virtue of these forms, through them and in them. As yet, however, the truth of these forms has never been considered or examined on their own account any more than their necessary interconnexion. (a) The Notion as Notion. The Notion as Notion contains the three following 'moments' or functional parts. (1) The first is Universality--meaning that it is in free equality with itself in its specific character. (2) The second is Particularity--that is, the specific character, in which the universal continues serenely equal to itself. (3) The third is Individuality--meaning the reflection-into-self of the specific characters of universality and particularity;--which negative self-unity has complete and original determinateness, without any loss to its self-identity or universality.

held_pairs.plain: This is merely a potential for damage. Yet the absence of real injury is no longer accidental, because the element of wrongdoing in private actions serves as the final basis for police authority. External realities exist within the infinite domain generated by the understanding, and therefore possess no natural limits. Consequently, no clear line can be drawn regarding what constitutes danger versus safety, suspicion versus innocence, prohibition versus monitoring, pardon with a warning versus retention under police watch, or dismissal on suspended sentence. Decisions rely on custom, the overall constitutional spirit, current conditions, immediate threats, and similar factors. No precise definition or absolute limit can be established here. Everything remains personal and shaped by subjective views. Any sharper distinctions stem from the constitutional spirit or the dangers of the era. For instance, during wartime, many morally neutral acts are treated as harmful. Due to this element of chance and arbitrary personal judgment, police face widespread disdain. They can use remote reasoning to bring any matter under their jurisdiction, since any situation may contain a potential for harm.
held_pairs.original: This is, indeed, only a possibility of harm. But that no actual injury is done is now no longer a matter of accident, since the aspect of wrong in private acts is the ultimate ground for the right of police control. The relations of external reality occur within the realm of the infinity created by the understanding, and have accordingly no inherent limit. Hence, as to what is dangerous and what not, what suspicious and what free from suspicion, what is to be forbidden, or kept under inspection, or pardoned with a reprimand, what is to be retained after pardon under police supervision, and what is to b'e dismissed on suspended sentence, no boundary can be laid down. Custom, the spirit of the constitution as a whole, the condition of the time, the danger of the moment, etc., furnish means for a decision. No fixed definition can here be given, or absolute boundary drawn. Here everything is personal and influenced by subjective opinion. To the spirit of the constitution or the danger of the times are due any more decisive characteristics. In time of war, e.g., many things morally harmless are looked on as harmful. Because of the presence of this aspect of contingency and arbitrary personality the police are viewed with odium. They can by far-fetched conclusions draw every kind of thing within their sphere; for in anything may be found a possibility of harm.

held_pairs.plain: Claiming, as we have done, that the mind and its artistic beauty rank above natural beauty is, in broad terms, hardly decisive. The term "higher" is completely vague. It treats natural and artistic beauty as if they merely sit next to each other in the realm of imagination. It presents the gap between them as a simple quantity, and thus as something purely external. However, when the mind and its artistic beauty are called "higher" than nature, they possess a distinction that is not merely relative. Only the mind can grasp truth. It contains everything that exists. Consequently, anything beautiful is genuinely and truly beautiful only when it shares in this superior element and is produced by it. In this way, natural beauty appears as just a mirror of the beauty inherent in the mind. It is an imperfect and incomplete way of existing. Its truly substantial content resides within the mind itself. Furthermore, limiting our focus to fine art seems very natural. Although much has been said, both by us and, to a lesser extent, by the ancients, about the beauty of nature, no one has ever thought to highlight the perspective of natural objects' beauty. No one has tried to build a science, or a systematic explanation, of these natural beauties.
held_pairs.original: To say, as we have said, in general terms, that mind and its artistic beauty stand higher than natural beauty, is no doubt to determine almost nothing. For "higher" is an utterly indefinite expression, which designates the beauty of nature and that of art as if merely standing side by side in the space of the imagination, and states the difference between them as purely quantitative, and, therefore, purely external. But the mind and its artistic beauty, in being "higher" as compared with nature, have a distinction which is not simply relative. Mind, and mind only, is capable of truth, and comprehends in itself all that is, so that whatever is beautiful can only be really and truly beautiful as partaking in this higher element and as created thereby. In this sense the beauty of nature reveals itself as but a reflection of the beauty which belongs to the mind, as an imperfect, incomplete mode of being, as a mode whose really substantial element is contained in the mind itself. Moreover, we shall find the restriction to fine art very natural, for however much has been and is said--though less by the ancients than by ourselves--of the beauties of nature, yet no one has taken it into his head to emphasize the point of view of the beauty of natural objects, and to attempt to make a science, a systematic account of these beauties.

held_pairs.plain: Reason is fully justified in holding this ground and rejecting the pull of mental constructs that merely should exist. It refuses to accept truth based on this "should," even if such things never appear in experience. It also rejects hypothetical hints and other intangible fictions created to serve an eternal "should" that never actually is. Reason is precisely the certainty of possessing reality. Therefore, anything this awareness does not recognize as an existing entity, meaning anything that does not show up, is nothing to this awareness at all. The true nature of law, which is essentially reality, will likely appear to awareness as an opposite to the concept and the inherently universal, provided awareness remains at the level of observation. In other words, this awareness does not view its law as a reality of reason; instead, it perceives the object as external and alien. However, it contradicts its own idea by failing to recognize that its universality does not require every individual sensory thing to have demonstrated the law before its truth can be claimed.
held_pairs.original: The instinct of reason is entirely within its rights when it stands firm on this point, and refuses to be led astray by entia intellectus which merely ought to be, and would have truth in the sense of this " ought to be," even though they are to be met with nowhere in experience; and dechnes to be turned aside by the hypothetical suggestions and all the other impalpable unreahties designed in the interest of an everlasting " ought to be " which never is. For reason is just this certainty of having reality, and what this consciousness is not aware of as an existent entity, i.e. what does not appear, is nothing for consciousness here at all. The true nature of law, viz.: that it essentially is reality, will, no doubt, again assume for consciousness, if it stops at the level of observation, the form of an opposite over against the notion and the inherently universal; in other words, this consciousness does not take such an object as its law to be a reality of reason; it ttinks it has got there something external and foreign. But it contradicts its own idea by actually and in fact not taking its universality to mean that all individual things of sense must have given evidence of the law to enable the truth of the law to be asserted.

held_pairs.plain: Cicero’s *Academics Quæstiones* preserves the core tenets of Arcesilaus’s thought, yet Sextus Empiricus serves as a superior source because his account is more exhaustive, precise, philosophical, and organized. a. We understand this system primarily as a dialectic aimed at Stoicism, a school with which Arcesilaus interacted extensively. Its central outcome is summarized by the rule that the wise individual must hold back their approval and agreement. This stance was termed ἐποχή, mirroring the Sceptic position. Conversely, this term links to Stoic doctrine in the following way. For Stoics, truth exists when thought claims a specific aspect of reality as its own, and the grasped concept validates that aspect. Consequently, the material of our concepts, principles, and ideas seems distinct from thought itself. The concrete unity of these two elements emerges only when a specific content is absorbed into the structure of thought, thereby manifesting as truth. Arcesilaus recognized this implication. His insistence on withholding approval effectively asserts that absorbing content in this manner yields no truth, merely appearance. This holds true because, as Arcesilaus argues, conception and thought remain separated.
held_pairs.original: The principal points in the philosophy of Arcesilaus are preserved by Cicero in his Academics Quæstiones, but Sextus Empiricus is more valuable as an authority, for he is more thorough, definite, philosophic and systematic. a. This philosophy is specially known to us as being a dialectic directed against Stoicism, with which Arcesilaus had much to do, and its result, as far as its main principles are concerned, is expressed thus: “The wise man must restrain his approbation and assent.” This principle was called ἐποχή, and it is the same as that of the Sceptics; on the other hand this expression is connected with the principle of the Stoics as follows. Because to Stoic philosophy truth consists in the fact that thought declares some content of existence to be its own, and the conception as comprehended gives its approbation to this content, the content of our conceptions, principles and thoughts undoubtedly appears to be different from thought, and the union of the two, which is the concrete, only arises by means of some determinate content being taken up into the form of thought and thus being expressed as the truth. But Arcesilaus saw this consequence, and his saying that approbation most be withheld is thus as much as saying that by thus taking up the content no truth comes to pass, but only phenomenon; and this is true, because, as Arcesilaus puts it, conception and thought likewise remain apart.

held_pairs.plain: My existence is directly tied to the act of thinking. Descartes claims this forms the ultimate foundation for all philosophy. The nature of existence is defined within my self; this link is the primary issue. Thinking is existence, and existence is thinking—this is my certainty, my self. In the famous statement "I think, therefore I am," thinking and existence are joined in an unbreakable bond. Some view this statement as a logical argument where existence is derived from thinking. Kant specifically argues against this, noting that existence is not included in the concept of thinking and is distinct from it. This distinction is valid, yet the two remain inseparable, forming a single identity. Their difference does not harm their unity. However, this rule of pure, abstract certainty—the complete whole where everything is implicitly present—is not proven. Therefore, we should not attempt to turn this statement into a logical argument. Descartes himself notes: "No logical argument is actually present."
held_pairs.original: The ‘I think’ directly involves my Being; this, says Descartes, is the absolute basis of all Philosophy. The determination of Being is in my ‘I’; this connection is itself the first matter. Thought as Being and Being as thought—that is my certainty, ‘I’; in the celebrated Cogito, ergo sum we thus have Thought and Being inseparably bound together. On the one hand this proposition is regarded as a syllogism: from thought Being is deduced. Kant more especially has objected to this that Being is not contained in thinking, that it is different from thinking. This is true, but they are still inseparable, or constitute an identity; their difference is not to the prejudice of their unity. Yet this maxim of pure abstract certainty, the universal totality in which everything implicitly exists, is not proved; we must therefore not try to convert this proposition into a syllogism. Descartes himself says: “There is no syllogism present at all.

held_pairs.plain: A self-assured spirit, taking the shape of a "beautiful soul," lacks the ability to let go of its isolated, non-communicative self-knowledge. Because it refuses to release this grip, it fails to merge with the consciousness it rejects. Consequently, it cannot perceive the unity of its own self within another life, nor can it achieve objective existence. Therefore, any equality that emerges is purely negative, representing a state stripped of spiritual quality. The "beautiful soul" thus lacks concrete reality. It persists within the tension between its pure self and the pressure this self feels to externalize itself and become actual. It dwells in the immediate, fixed opposition of this tension. This immediacy serves as the sole middle term, mediating and reconciling an opposition that has reached pure abstraction, which is equivalent to pure being or empty nothingness. Since the "beautiful soul" remains aware of this contradiction in its unreconciled immediacy, it becomes unstable, disordered, and descends into madness. It fades away in longing and is consumed by pining starvation. In doing so, it factually abandons its rigid claim to separate, independent existence. However, this abandonment only produces the soulless, spiritless unity of abstract being.
held_pairs.original: Now, so far as the spirit which is certain of itself, in the form of a " beautiful soul," does not possess the faculty of relinquishing the self-absorbed uncommunicative knowledge of itself, it cannot attain to any identity with the consciousness that is repulsed, and so cannot succeed in seeing the unity of its self in another hfe, cannot reach objective existence. The equahty comes about, therefore, merely in a negative way, as a state of being devoid of spiritual character. The "beautiful soul," then, has no concrete reahty; it subsists in the contradiction between its pure self and the necessity felt by this self to externalise itself and turn into something actual; it exists in the immediacy of this rooted and fixed opposition, an immediacy which alone is the middle term mediating and reconciling an opposition which has arisen to its pure abstraction, and is pure being or empty nothingness. Thus the " beautiful soul," being conscious of this contradiction in its unreconciled immediacy, is unhinged, disordered, and runs to madness, passes away in yearning, and is consimied in pining inanition. Thereby it gives up, as a fact, its stubborn insistence on its own isolated self-existence, but only to bring forth the soulless, spiritless unity of abstract being.

held_pairs.plain: All around us, a chaotic mix of events pulls us into their sphere of influence, and as soon as one set of circumstances disappears, another takes its place right away. The broad concept that first emerges from this constant shifting of individuals and nations, which exist for a while and then cease to be, is the idea of change in general. Looking at the remains of an old empire immediately directs our attention to this notion of change from a negative perspective. Which traveler visiting the ruins of Carthage, Palmyra, Persepolis, or Rome has not been prompted to think about the temporary nature of states and people, and to feel sorrow for a strong and abundant existence that is now gone? This is not a sadness focused on personal losses or the unpredictability of one’s own projects, but rather an impartial grief over the decline of a magnificent and highly developed national culture.
held_pairs.original: On every hand there is the motliest throng of events drawing us within the circle of its interest, and when one combination vanishes another immediately appears in its place. The general thought — the category which first presents itself in this restless mutation of individuals and peoples, existing for a time and then vanishing — is that of change at large. The sight of the ruins of some ancient sovereignty directly leads us to contemplate this thought of change in its negative aspect. What traveller among the ruins of Carthage, of Palmyra, Persepolis, or Rome, has not been stimulated to reflections on the transiency of kingdoms and men, and to sadness at the thought of a vigorous and rich life now departed— a sadness which does not expend itself on personal losses and the uncertainty of one's own undertakings, but is a disinterested sorrow at the decay of a splendid and highly cultured national life!

held_pairs.plain: Melitus claimed he had advised certain individuals to follow his guidance instead of their parents. This specific charge targeted Anytus primarily. Because Melitus provided adequate witnesses to support his claim, the law considered the point proven. However, without a sensible person nearby to supervise him, the young man would develop bad impulses and fall into reckless behavior. Xenophon noted that Socrates’ forecast had come true exactly as stated. The youth devoted himself to drinking, consuming alcohol from morning until night, and became completely corrupt. This outcome is easy to grasp. A person who believes they are suited for higher pursuits, whether that belief is accurate or not, suffers from internal conflict. They feel unhappy with their current situation but see no way to improve it. This frustration leads to apathy, which paves the path toward the destructive habits that frequently destroy people. Therefore, Socrates’ prediction was entirely logical.
held_pairs.original: “Melitus said that he knew some whom he advised to obey him rather than their parents,” This point of the accusation principally related to Anytus, and since he made it good by sufficient testimony, the point was undoubtedly proved, in accordance with law. Nevertheless, because he had no rational person near to look after him, he would come to have evil desires and be brought into dissolute ways. Xenophon added that Socrates’ prophecy had come to pass literally, and that the young man gave himself up to drink, and drank day and night, becoming totally depraved. This can be easily understood, for a man who feels himself to be fit for something better (whether truly so or not) and through this discord in his mind is discontented with the circumstances in which he lives, yet capable of attaining to no other, is led out of this disgust into listlessness, and is thus on the way to the evil courses which so often ruin men. The prediction of Socrates is thus quite natural.

held_pairs.plain: In habitual existence, a person’s way of being is "natural," which makes it unfree. Yet it remains free to the extent that habit reduces the purely natural aspect of feeling to a simple state of being. The individual is no longer pulled or pushed involuntarily by these feelings, nor are they concerned, engaged, or reliant upon them. The lack of freedom in habit is partly just a matter of form, since habit merely connects to the soul’s state. It is also partly relative, because it truly appears only with bad habits, or when a habit clashes with another aim. In contrast, the habit of rightness and goodness embodies liberty. The key aspect of Habit is that it frees people from their feelings, even while they are experiencing them. These variations can be outlined as follows: (α) The immediate feeling is denied and viewed as irrelevant. Someone who becomes accustomed to external sensations (cold, heat, limb fatigue, etc., pleasant tastes, etc.), and who toughens their heart against bad luck, gains a strength. This strength means that although the cold, etc.—or the bad luck—is sensed, the emotional impact is reduced to a mere external and immediate fact. The broader mental life maintains its own abstract independence within this, and the sense of self, awareness, reflection, and any other goals or actions are no longer disturbed by it.
held_pairs.original: In habit the human being’s mode of existence is “natural,” and for that reason not free; but still free, so far as the merely natural phase of feeling is by habit reduced to a mere being of his, and he is no longer involuntarily attracted or repelled by it, and so no longer interested, occupied, or dependent in regard to it. The want of freedom in habit is partly merely formal, as habit merely attaches to the being of the soul; partly only relative, so far as it strictly speaking arises only in the case of bad habits, or so far as a habit is opposed by another purpose: whereas the habit of right and goodness is an embodiment of liberty. The main point about Habit is that by its means man gets emancipated from the feelings, even in being affected by them. The different forms of this may be described as follows: (α) The immediate feeling is negated and treated as indifferent. One who gets inured against external sensations (frost, heat, weariness of the limbs, &c., sweet tastes, &c.), and who hardens the heart against misfortune, acquires a strength which consists in this, that although the frost, &c.—or the misfortune—is felt, the affection is deposed to a mere externality and immediacy; the universal psychical life keeps its own abstract independence in it, and the self-feeling as such, consciousness, reflection, and any other purposes and activity, are no longer bothered with it.

held_pairs.plain: What people label as demonstrations of God’s existence are, when properly grasped, methods for describing and breaking down the mind’s inherent trajectory. This is the path where thinking processes sensory input. When thought moves past the sensory realm, shifting from the limited to the boundless, and making a jump into the non-sensory by breaking the link to the senses, this entire shift is purely thought. If you claim this shift does not happen, you are claiming that thinking itself does not occur. Indeed, animals do not make this shift. They never go beyond sensation and sensory perception, and as a result, they possess no religion. There are two points to raise regarding the critique of this elevation in thought, both in general terms and in this specific instance. The first point addresses the issue of form.
held_pairs.original: And what men call the proofs of God's existence are, rightly understood, ways of describing and analysing the native course of the mind, the course of thought thinking the data of the senses. The rise of thought beyond the world of sense, its passage from the finite to the infinite, the leap into the super-sensible which it takes when it snaps asunder the chain of sense, all this transition is thought and nothing but thought. Say there is no such passage, and you say there is to be no thinking. And in sooth, animals make no such transition. They never get further than sensation and the perception of the senses, and in consequence they have no religion. Both on general grounds, and in the particular case, there are two remarks to be made upon the criticism of this exaltation in thought. The first remark deals with the question of form.

held_pairs.plain: Marriage creates a fresh household that stands on its own, distinct from the ancestral lines it originated from. While blood ties link this new unit to those older branches, ethical love serves as its core foundation. Consequently, a person’s assets are fundamentally tied to their marriage rather than to their birth lineage. When couples agree to limit shared ownership or preserve the wife’s separate rights, they do so to protect against the marriage ending through death or separation. Such provisions ensure that family members receive their designated portions of the shared property if the union dissolves. Many legal systems still emphasize the broader kinship network. They view this wider circle as the true unifying force, treating the immediate household as relatively minor. For instance, under ancient Roman law, a woman in a loose marriage remained closer to her own kin than to her spouse and offspring. Similarly, during the feudal era, the drive to maintain family prestige meant only male descendants were counted within the lineage. In these cases, the entire kinship network took priority, overshadowing the new household. Despite this, each new household remains more fundamental than the wider group defined by blood relations.
held_pairs.original: Marriage establishes a new family, which has its own independent footing as against the stems or houses from, which it has proceeded. The connection of the new family with these stems is consanguinity, but the principle of the new family is ethical love. Thus, the individual's property is essentially allied to his marriage, and less intimately to his original stock or house. A marriage-settlement, which imposes a limit to the common possession of goods by the wedded couple, or any other arrangement by which the right of the wife is retained, is intended to be security against the dissolution of the marriage-tie by death or divorce. In such an event the different members of the family are by this arrangement apportioned their shares of the common possession. In many law codes the more extended range of the family circle is retained. It is looked upon as the real bond of union, while the tie of the single family is regarded as comparatively unimportant. Thus in the older Eoman law the wife of the lax marriage is more closely allied to her relatives than to her husband and children. In feudal times, also, the necessity of preserving the splendor famdliae led to reckoning under the family only its male members. Thus the whole family connection was the chief object of concern, and the newly-formed family was placed in the background. Notwithstanding this, every new family is more essential than the vidder circle bounded by the tie of consanguinity.

held_pairs.plain: Art starts closer to the mind and its thinking processes than does raw, unthinking external nature. In artistic creations, the mind deals only with its own substance. Even though art is not abstract thought or concept, but rather a development of the concept out of itself, a separation from itself toward the sensory world, the power of the thinking spirit remains present. This power allows the spirit to recognize itself not only in its specific form as self-consciousness, but also in its separated state, appearing as feeling and sensory experience. By transforming this changed thought back into clear ideas, the spirit restores itself. In this focus on its own opposite, the thinking spirit does not betray itself, nor does it forget or give itself up. It is not so weak that it cannot understand what is different from itself. Instead, it understands both itself and its opposite. The concept is universal, maintaining itself within its specific forms. It controls both itself and its "other." It becomes the power and activity that ends the separation it created. Therefore, the artwork where thought separates itself belongs, like thought itself, to the domain of understanding thought. When the mind examines this scientifically, it simply fulfills a need of its deepest nature.
held_pairs.original: In this respect art is, to begin with, nearer to mind and its thinking activity than is mere external unintelligent nature; in works of art, mind has to do but with its own. And even if artistic works are not abstract thought and notion, but are an evolution of the notion out of itself, an alienation from itself towards the sensuous, still the power of the thinking spirit (mind) lies herein, not merely to grasp itself only in its peculiar form of the self-conscious spirit (mind), but just as much to recognize itself in its alienation in the shape of feeling and the sensuous, in its other form, by transmuting the metamorphosed thought back into definite thoughts, and so restoring it to itself. And in this preoccupation with the other of itself the thinking spirit is not to be held untrue to itself as if forgetting or surrendering itself therein, nor is it so weak as to lack strength to comprehend what is different from itself, but it comprehends both itself and its opposite. For the notion is the universal, which preserves itself in its particularizations, dominates alike itself and its "other," and so becomes the power and activity that consists in undoing the alienation which it had evolved. And thus the work of art in which thought alienates itself belongs, like thought itself, to the realm of comprehending thought, and the mind, in subjecting it to scientific consideration, is thereby but satisfying the want of its own inmost nature.

held_pairs.plain: The Idea, which is undoubtedly true in its own right, never progresses beyond its initial point as long as its development consists solely of repeating identical formulas. When the knowing subject transports this single, inert, abstract form everywhere, externally collecting whatever material it encounters and immersing it in this element, the result approximates the desired outcome—specifically, the self-generation of detailed wealth and the self-determination of shape and form distinctions—as closely as random conjectures about the relevant content. This is essentially a monotonous formalism that only achieves variation in the subject matter it processes because that material is already prepared and familiar. This monotony and abstract universality are posited as the Absolute. This formalism maintains that dissatisfaction with it reveals an inability to comprehend the Absolute's standpoint and maintain a secure grasp of it.
held_pairs.original: The Idea, which by itself is no doubt the truth, really never gets any farther than just where it began, as long as the development of it consists in nothing else than such a repetition of the same formula. If the knowing subject carries round everywhere the one inert abstract form, taking up in external fashion whatever material comes his way, and dipping it into this element, then this comes about as near to fulfilhng what is wanted — viz. a selforigination of the wealth of detail, and a self- determining distinction of shapes and forms — as any chance fancies about the content in question. It is rather a monotonous formalism, which only comes by distinction in the matter it has to deal with, because this is already prepared and well known. This monotonousness and abstract universality are maintained to be the Absolute. This formalism insists that to be dissatisfied therewith argues an incapacity to grasp the standpoint of the Absolute, and keep a firm hold on it.

held_pairs.plain: Philo produced an extensive body of work, much of which remains available today. Examples include texts on world creation, rewards and punishments, those who offer sacrifices, the law of allegories, dreams, and the unchanging nature of God. These works appeared in folio format in Frankfort in 1691, followed later by a publication from Pfeiffer in Erlangen. Philo gained renown for the vast scope of his knowledge and his deep familiarity with Greek philosophical traditions. He is particularly noted for his engagement with Platonic thought and for his diligent efforts to prove that philosophy exists within the Jewish sacred texts. When interpreting the history of the Jewish people, the actual events and statements in those narratives no longer held their direct, real-world significance for him. Instead, he consistently attributed mystical and allegorical meanings to them, effectively locating Plato within the writings of Moses. Essentially, Philo’s approach mirrored that of the Alexandrians, who identified philosophical doctrines within Greek myths. He discussed the nature of Mind not as something contained within the realm of thought, but as something expressed through it. This expression remained impure and was intertwined with various images. Driven by the spirit of Philosophy, Jews were forced to look for deeper speculative meanings in their holy books, similar to how pagans sought them in Homer and common religious practices. Consequently, they presented their religious writings as a complete system of divine wisdom.
held_pairs.original: Philo wrote a long series of works, many of which we still possess; for instance, those on The Creation of the World, on Rewards and Punishments, the Offerers of Sacrifices, the Law of Allegories, Dreams, the Immutability of God, &c.; they were published in folio at Frankfort in 1691, and afterwards by Pfeiffer at Erlangen. Philo was famous for the great extent of his learning, and was well acquainted with Greek philosophy. He is more especially distinguished for his Platonic philosophy, and also for the pains he took to demonstrate the presence of Philosophy in the sacred writings of the Jews. In his explanation of the history of the Jewish nation, the narratives and statements therein contained have lost for him the immediate significance of reality. He reads into them throughout a mystical and allegorical meaning, and finds Plato present in Moses; in short, the endeavour of Philo resembled that of the Alexandrians when they recognized philosophic dogmas in Greek mythology. He treats of the nature of Mind, not, indeed, as comprehended in the element of thought, but as expressed therein, and this expression is still both far from pure and is associated with all sorts of imageries. By the spirit of Philosophy the Jews were compelled to seek in their sacred books, as the heathen sought in Homer and in the popular religion, a deeper speculative meaning, and to represent their religious writings as a perfect system of divine wisdom.

held_pairs.plain: God’s primary quality is that He is truthful and the source of all illumination. Therefore, it is completely opposed to His character to mislead us. Consequently, the natural light, or the capacity for gaining understanding that God granted us, cannot interact with any subject that is not genuinely true, specifically in the way it is engaged by that capacity. This refers to how things are perceived clearly and distinctly. We attribute truthfulness to God. Based on this, Descartes deduces the universal link between absolute knowledge and the objective nature of what we know through it. Knowledge possesses objects and a content that is understood; we label this relationship as truth. God’s truthfulness is precisely this union of what the subject thinks or perceives clearly, and external reality or existence. This concludes the possibility of doubt, as though what seems entirely obvious to us might not actually be true. We can therefore no longer suspect mathematical truths. Similarly, if we pay attention to what we distinguish through our senses while awake or asleep, clearly and distinctly, it is straightforward to identify the true aspects of each thing.
held_pairs.original: “Now the first attribute of God is that He is true and the Giver of all light; it is hence quite contrary to His nature to deceive us. Hence the light of nature or the power of acquiring knowledge given us by God can affect no object which is not really true in as far as it is affected by it” (the power of acquiring knowledge) “i.e. as it is perceived clearly and distinctly.” We ascribe truth to God. From this Descartes goes on to infer the universal bond which exists between absolute knowledge and the objectivity of what we thus know. Knowledge has objects, has a content which is known; we call this connection truth. The truth of God is just this unity of what is thought by the subject or clearly perceived, and external reality or existence. “Thereby an end is put to doubt, as if it could be the case that what appears quite evident to us should not be really true. We can thus no longer have any suspicion of mathematical truths. Likewise if we give heed to what we distinguish by our senses in waking or in sleeping, clearly and distinctly, it is easy to recognize in each thing what in it is true.”

held_pairs.plain: Against this inward shaping stands the factor of being, the all-encompassing awareness. For this latter, the essential reality is rather the universal and the obligatory. Individuality, which exists for its own sake and opposes the universal, holds only the worth of a passed phase. The awareness that stands with the fact of obligation regards the initial awareness as wicked, because its inner subjective life lacks alignment or oneness with the universal. Since the initial awareness simultaneously claims its action to be one with itself, to be obligation and sincerity, that all-encompassing awareness regards it as deceit. The path of this conflict begins with the formal restoration of the oneness between what the wicked awareness essentially is and what it claims to be. It must be shown that it is wicked, and its objective presence must be brought into alignment with its true nature; the deceit must be exposed.
held_pairs.original: Over against this internal determination there thus stands the element of existence, the universal consciousness; and for this latter it is rather universality, duty, which is the essential fact, while individuality, which exists for itself and is opposed to the imiversal, has merely the value of a superseded moment. The first consciousness is held to be Evil by the consciousness which thus stands by the fact of duty, because of the lack of congruity or identity of its internal subjective Ufe with the universal; and since at the same time the first consciousness declares its act to be identity with itself, to be duty and conscientiousness, it is held by that universal consciousness to be Uyfocrisy. The course taken by this opposition is, in the first instance, the formal reinstatement of the identity between what the evil consciousness is in its own nature and what it declares itself to be. It has to be made manifest that it is evil, and its objective existence thus made congruent with its real nature; the hypocrisy must be unmasked.

held_pairs.ref: The Greek World, The Peloponnesian War
held_pairs.plain: The Greek ideal of liberty inherently contains the liberation of thinking. We saw the first stirrings of thought among the group previously identified by their famous title, the Seven Sages. These individuals were the first to voice universal statements, even though wisdom back then relied more on direct, concrete understanding of things rather than the ability to form abstract concepts. As religious art and political structures evolved, thinking grew stronger, acting as both a rival and a dismantler of those forms. By the era of the Peloponnesian War, scientific knowledge had already advanced significantly. The Sophists initiated the practice of reflecting on current conditions and engaging in logical reasoning. The same energy and diligence we saw in Greek daily life and artistic creation appeared in the complex paths these ideas followed. Just as physical objects are altered, processed, and repurposed for uses different from their original intent, the core nature of Spirit—what is thought and known—gets manipulated in various ways. It becomes a subject for the mind to engage with, and this engagement turns into an interest that exists for its own sake. The internal movement of thought, which operates within its own domain without relying on outside objects, a process that previously held no appeal, now gains value purely on its own merits.
held_pairs.original: In the principle of Greek Freedom, inasmuch as it is Freedom, is involved the self-emancipation of Thought. "We observed the dawn of Thought in the circle of men mentioned above under their well-known appellation of the Seven Sages. It was they who first uttered general propositions; though at that time wisdom consisted rather in a concrete insight [into things, than in the power of abstract conception]. Parallel with the advance in the development of Religious Art and with political growth, we find a progressive strengthening of Thought, its enemy and destroyer; and at the time of the Pelopounesian War science was already developed. With the Sophists began the process of reflection on the existing state of things, and of ratiocination. That very diligence and activity which we observed among the Greeks in their practical life, and in the achievement of works of art, shewed itself also in the turns and windings which these ideas took; so that, as material things are changed, worked up and used for other than their original purposes, similarly the essential being of Spirit — what is thought and known — is variously handled; it is made an object about which the mind can employ itself, and this occupation becomes an interest in and for itself. The movement of Thought — that which goes on within its sphere [without reference to an extrinsic object] — a process which had formerly no interest — acquires attractiveness on its own account.
